Hi Emma / team,

Attached are the artifacts requested: a high-level east-west controls diagram and a concise threat-model summary. Below is a targeted summary answering the bullets you called out. If you want additional depth we can follow up with design-level diagrams.

1) Topology & separation
- Control plane: hosted in a dedicated VPC/tenant in our control plane region. Management APIs, orchestration, and billing are logically separated from customer compute. Control-plane access is over dedicated management endpoints and uses mutual TLS with client certificates.
- Data plane: customer workloads run in isolated tenant VPCs or private subnets (depending on Private vs Dedicated mode). Tenants have distinct network namespaces and iptables/eBPF policies enforced at the host and virtual network layer.

2) East-west enforcement points
- Per-host enforcement: an eBPF-based host firewall enforces deny-by-default microsegmentation for pod-to-pod flows. Policies are derived from route tables and service-level RBAC.
- Network policies: we apply security groups and VPC-level ACLs to restrict permitted ports and CIDR ranges. We also support AWS PrivateLink/Private Service Connect patterns for private integrations.
- Service mesh / mTLS: internal service-to-service traffic is authenticated and encrypted using mTLS (mutual TLS) with short-lived certificates minted by our internal PKI.

3) KV cache & GPU isolation
- KV caches are namespaced per-tenant; eviction/TTL policies and prefix separation ensure no shared in-memory keys across tenants. Critical caches are stored in per-tenant Redis instances (or namespaced shards) depending on contract.
- GPU jobs: workloads run in per-tenant GPU pools where feasible. Both logical scheduling (quota enforcement) and listing-level isolation (container namespaces + cgroups + device assignment) are used. For Dedicated and Private customers we can provide pinned GPU nodes to prevent noisy neighbor risk.

4) Logging, audit, and key management
- Audit logs: every management action and tenant API call is logged to an immutable append-only stream. Customers may ingest logs into their own SIEM using a dedicated log stream or we can push to a customer S3/GCS bucket.
- Encryption: all data in transit is TLS 1.3; at-rest encryption uses customer-managed keys (KMS/HSM) for Private deployments and a KMS with dedicated key per-tenant for Dedicated.

5) Threat model highlights (summary)
- Likely lateral-movement vectors we mitigate: compromised control-plane credential, misconfigured network policy, compromised build pipeline. Mitigations include: RBAC with least privilege, mandatory mTLS for internal traffic, automated policy-compliance scans, and periodic end-to-end penetration testing. See attached one-page threat summary for enumerated attack paths and detection signals.

6) Access & operational procedures
- Operator access is gated through jump hosts with MFA, TOTP, and just-in-time elevation. Privileged sessions are recorded.
- For Private customers we offer an air-gapped deployment option and a customer-controlled KMS/HSM integration.

Kimberly — thanks for the fast and detailed response, and for the attachments. A few clarifying questions from our architects:

- KV cache: you note per-tenant namespacing and per-tenant Redis options. Can you confirm the default hosted model in Redwood's public offering — is there ever a shared in-memory cache between tenants?
- GPU job isolation: for multi-tenant pools, do you use hardware-level partitioning or is it strictly scheduler/namespace-level isolation? Any side-channel mitigation guidance (e.g., frequency/power controls)?
- Audit logs: which retention options are configurable per-customer in the hosted API? Who can request export to an external SIEM?
- Do you support FedRAMP / AWS GovCloud regions for US-government workloads?

If you can reply inline it will help our procurement team include the clarifications in the RFP.

Hi Emma — quick inline answers below and an extra attachment that shows a snippet of the KV cache isolation rules we apply.

- KV cache: In the Redwood hosted (standard) offering the default is isolated namespaces within a managed cache cluster; we do not place unrelated customer data into the same in-memory keyspace. For customers with stricter requirements we offer per-tenant managed Redis instances (dedicated shards) as an upgrade. The default ensures tenant keys are namespaced + ACL enforced at the proxy layer.

- GPU isolation: Multi-tenant pools use scheduler/namespace isolation + cgroups + device assignment; we do not claim hardware-enforced partitioning in the standard shared pool. For customers who require hardware separation we provide pinned nodes or Dedicated GPU pools. Regarding side channels, our recommendations are: 1) use dedicated GPU nodes for sensitive workloads, 2) enable constant-time kernels when available, and 3) avoid co-locating high-sensitivity workloads with untrusted tenants. We also offer CPU/GPU frequency governor configuration in Private deployments.

- Audit log retention & export: For hosted API customers retention is configurable between 30/90/365 days by tier. Exports to an external SIEM (S3/GCS or direct SIEM forwarders) are enabled via API and require a customer admin or an authorized Redwood integrations engineer to configure the destination. We can provision a dedicated log stream per-customer for real-time ingest.

- FedRAMP / GovCloud: We support Private deployments in AWS GovCloud and can run our control plane in a FedRAMP-eligible configuration for deeply regulated customers. For full FedRAMP authorization we work with partners and can provide a deployment plan and timeline.
